text: Rust is well known for its memory safety, performance and reliability, but for developers building real-world applications, the ecosystem of libraries is just as important as the language itself. Over the years, Rust has grown from a language focused mainly on systems programming into a powerful ecosystem for backend development, command line tools, networking, data processing, and much more. Along the way, the Rust community has built an impressive collection of libraries known as crates that make development faster and more productive. In today's video, we're going to explore some interesting Rust libraries that are worth knowing about. First on our list is rerun, an open source visualization library built in Rust that helps developers understand complex data in real time. It's particularly useful in robotics, computer vision, and machine learning, where debugging raw sensor data can be challenging. With rerun, you can visualize images, 3D point clouds, sensor readings, and time series data in a single interactive viewer. You can stream data live or record it and replay it later. For example, if you're developing a robot, rerun lets you visualize what its camera's capture, track its movements, and inspect sensor readings, all synchronized on a timeline. It also provides SDKs for Python and C++, making it useful beyond Rust projects. Next is GPUI Kit, an open source Rust framework for building modern, high-performance desktop applications. It's built on top of GPUI, the GPU accelerated UI framework, developed by the team behind the Z code editor. GPUI Kit provides over 75 ready-to-use components and primitives, including buttons, forms, data tables, navigation menus, and customizable layouts. This means developers can build polished interfaces without creating every UI component from scratch. It also includes more advanced features like virtual scrolling, dockable panels, and a built-in code editor with syntax highlighting. GPUI Kit supports Windows, Mac OS, and Linux, making it an interesting choice for building cross-platform desktop software entirely in Rust. Next is this error, a lightweight Rust library that makes defining and handling custom errors much easier. In Rust, errors are often represented using enums, but implementing the standard error trait and formatting messages manually can involve repetitive code. This error simplifies that process with a drive macro. By simply adding this to your error types, it automatically generates the necessary trait implementations. You can also define readable error messages and automatically convert between compatible error types using simple attributes. For example, in a backend application, you can define separate errors for database failures, invalid inputs, or missing resources while keeping your error handling code clean and organized. Next is Pingora, an open-source Rust framework developed by Cloudflare for building fast, secure, and customizable network services. Cloudflare originally built Pingora to replace its proxy infrastructure. By the time it was open-sourced in 2024, Pingora had already handled nearly a quadrillion internet requests across Cloudflare's global network. Built around an asynchronous multi-threaded architecture, Pingora provides the tools needed to build HTTP proxies, load balancers, and network gateways. It supports HTTP1 and HTTP2, TLS encryption, connection pooling, and customizable load balancing strategies. One of its most useful features is its programmable API, which lets developers control how requests are routed, modified, or forwarded to backend servers. Pingora also supports graceful restarts without dropping incoming requests, making it particularly valuable for production infrastructure. Another interesting library worth exploring is Ratatouille, an open-sourced Rust library for building interactive terminal user interfaces, commonly known as TUIs. Instead of limiting your command line applications to plain text and basic prompts, Ratatouille lets you build rich interfaces directly inside the terminal. It provides a collection of ready-to-use widgets like tables, lists, charts, gauges, and progress bars, along with a flexible layout system for organizing them on the screen. Under the hood, Ratatouille is an immediate mode rendering approach. Your application redraws the interface based on its current state, while Ratatouille compares frames and updates only the parts of the terminal that have changed. It also works with terminal backends like cross-term to support keyboard and mouse interactions. Whether you're building a system monitoring dashboard, an interactive Git tool, or a terminal based developer utility, Ratatouille gives you the building blocks to create polished applications entirely in Rust. Moving into database development, we have Diesel, a powerful ORM and query builder for working with relational databases in Rust. One common problem with database libraries is that certain query mistakes only become visible at runtime, when the application actually communicates with the database. Diesel takes a different approach. It uses Rust's powerful type system to check queries during compilation, catching many mistakes before your application even runs. For example, if you try to query a column that doesn't exist in your defined schema, or insert a string into an integer column, Diesel's type safe query builder will reject the code at compilation time. This helps developers catch database-related bugs earlier, and reduces the chances of unexpected failures in production. Those are some of my picks for today's video, but you can explore many more useful Rust libraries in the GitHub repositories I've linked in the description below. [BLANK_AUDIO]
